title: Case debrief: defend your diagnosis of TTF to the PM
rubric: Opens with the conclusion in one sentence: the TTF level behaves like a unit-root (I(1)) process; daily log returns are stationary; the analysis works on returns.
Gives the evidence with the right nulls: ADF on the level cannot reject a unit root (p ≈ 0.91), KPSS rejects stationarity (p ≤ 0.01) — and the reverse on returns.
Explains why the level's mean and standard deviation are not meaningful (they wander with the sample) and quotes risk on returns (≈ 2.1 % a day, fat tails, excess kurtosis ≈ 4).
Says what the tests do NOT establish: a non-rejection is not proof; stationary returns do not mean constant volatility or predictability.
Names the main limits: three years of data (power), possible breaks, results under the chosen specification ('c', no deterministic trend visible).
Contrasts with a trend-stationary series (diesel demand): not every trend calls for differencing — shows the choice was reasoned, not automatic.
States what would change the conclusion or what comes next (e.g. a visible break → sub-period tests; a relationship with another price → cointegration, Case 3).
